text: Reading Three · Burt & Whitney (2018) From Resource Room to the Real World: Facilitating Generalization Eddie and Mrs. Claire 1 Eddie is a sixth-grade student with a specific learning disability in reading. At his annual IEP meeting, his general education teacher reported that Eddie was not keeping up with his independent classwork. 2 In social studies Eddie often sits quietly at his desk and pretends to complete the assignment by copying irrelevant text from his book. In math and science, he writes random answers without engaging the content as instructed. 3 Even though Eddie has been taught how to request help by his special education teacher, he was not transferring this skill to his general education classes. Asked why, Eddie said he doesn't know when or how to get help from his teachers — they always look so busy. 4 Mrs. Claire, his special education teacher, wonders why Eddie raises his hand for help in the resource classroom but not in his general education classes. "What can I do to encourage Eddie to transfer this skill to where it matters most?" Many special education teachers have encountered challenges similar to Mrs. Claire's. Teaching a skill within the highly controlled conditions of one setting and promoting the transfer of that skill to a less-structured setting may seem like an unattainable goal. Yet this is the challenge presented by many IEP objectives that involve generalization of a skill acquired in a resource room to be applied outside of it — indeed, it is a challenge for any learning task where one environment is selected for initial skill acquisition with the expectation that the behavior occurs elsewhere. The ability to generalize skills across settings is essential at all stages of life for nearly every learned skill. Although generalization, or generality as it is sometimes called, is one of the most important outcomes of applied behavioral interventions (Cooper, Heron, & Heward, 2007), it frequently fails to occur naturally following initial intervention efforts. In other words, generalization is not guaranteed. The challenges associated with the lack of generalization were first articulated by Baer, Wolf, and Risley (1968); fortunately, progress has been made toward the development of systematic generalization promotion strategies (Osnes & Lieblein, 2003). In 1977, Stokes and Baer defined generalization as the extension of behavior change across "different, nontraining conditions (i.e., across subjects, settings, people, behaviors, and/or time) without the scheduling of the same events in those conditions as had been scheduled in the training conditions" (p. 350). Generalization is observed when behavior change accomplished under certain conditions, targeting a specific behavior and with specific students, is subsequently observed in different settings (e.g., from a resource room to a general education classroom), with novel people, with new behaviors, and at a different time (maintenance or follow-up). The Council for Exceptional Children and the CEEDAR Center published a collection of 22 high-leverage practices described as essential to promoting improved outcomes for students with disabilities; one of these is to "teach students to maintain and generalize new learning across time and settings" (HLP 21; McLeskey et al., 2017). The domains of generalization Domain Definition Example Setting or situation Appropriate responding in new or novel environmental conditions Teaching students a strategy to answer mathematics word problems in the resource room, which is then applied during mathematics class; teaching students to say "hello" to you, and then students start saying "hello" to other teachers Response Variety of behaviors that are altered or changed as a result of direct training of a specific response Praising students for writing their names neatly at the top of the paper, and the handwriting on the rest of the assignment improves; reminding students as they enter the bathroom to wash their hands, and in the process they also throw away their paper towels Time Student maintains correct responding when parts or all of the instructional supports are removed (maintenance) or following extended periods after instruction ends (follow-up) Student uses a problem-solving mnemonic even though the poster with the mnemonic has been removed; hand-raising in the general education classroom continues after verbal reminders have been removed Participants Students not directly involved in the training interactions demonstrate acquisition of the skill After seeing the poster, other students begin using a mnemonic that was taught to the target student; other students start raising their hands after hearing the target student being reinforced Stokes and Osnes (1989) organized the strategies first summarized by Stokes and Baer (1977) into three generalization promotion categories: train diversely, exploit functional contingencies, and incorporate functional mediators. Train diversely Teaching procedures that call for a narrow range of specific responses are not likely to generalize to new environments. Similarly, an instructional setting that is too repetitive and predictable may result in overly tight instructional control: a student is more likely to perform a learned behavior in generalization settings only if that setting closely mirrors the initial teaching conditions. For example, Eddie's initial advocacy training in the resource room consisted of Mrs. Claire presenting independent worksheets, modeling hand raising, then prompting Eddie to do the same; each time Eddie raised his hand, Mrs. Claire immediately attended to his question. Eddie quickly mastered this skill in five consecutive trials — but repetitive instruction in this case likely produced overly restricted behavior patterns. Use a variety of stimulus and response examples Stimulus examples are the prompts that occur before the behavior; response examples are the various forms of behavior targeted in instruction. To maximize the probability of generalization, it is important to incorporate a variety of both. The method of  general case instruction  developed by Horner and colleagues in the 1980s helps to formalize this process: it involves a systematic assessment of the various stimulus arrangements likely encountered in a student's natural environment and presentation of a sample of that range during instruction. It is not practical, or in many cases even possible, to incorporate every stimulus example a student will encounter; the goal is to efficiently teach a skill by minimizing the number of examples needed while maximizing the probability of correct responding when confronted with new but similar problems. When implementing general case instruction, it is also important to consider the range of situations in which a new response would  not  be appropriate — overgeneralization. It is appropriate for Eddie to raise his hand for assistance during independent work with challenging tasks; raising his hand in the middle of group instruction for unrelated questions is not. There is no formula for determining the scope of generalization in every situation. If a circumstance arises in which overgeneralization occurs, teachers must simply address it by incorporating the scenario in another round of instruction. Step Eddie's example 1. Define the range of generalization settings Eddie will use self-advocacy skills (asking for teacher assistance) in general education classrooms, including special areas, during independent activities 2. List all relevant stimulus activities, setting circumstances, and response examples Stimulus activities:  independent activities, including worksheets, computer or tablet assignments, teacher-assigned tasks with textbooks, and projects involving tangibles or manipulatives.  Setting circumstances:  teacher available, teacher busy helping other students, teacher busy with other tasks.  Response:  hand raising, vocal interjection, stand and wait, cue cards 3. List potential areas for overgeneralization Hand raising in Mr. Harris's room is forbidden 4. Select and sequence teaching examples Hand raising during an independent worksheet when the teacher is available; vocal interjection during a textbook task when the teacher is busy with other tasks; stand and wait during a computer assignment when the teacher is busy with other students; cue card during a manipulative assignment when the teacher is available 5. Deliver instruction with progress monitoring Outline rationale and steps; model the technique for each stimulus and setting example; provide guided practice; give positive or corrective feedback; record student performance in table or graph format Make antecedents and consequences less discriminable A second reason teaching procedures may fail to produce generalization is that students often attempt a strategy only if they are aware that reinforcement for that behavior is available and likely to occur. During initial training in the resource room, Eddie raised his hand for every trial and received immediate feedback each time — the positive consequence was highly likely and highly discriminable. General education teachers, by contrast, frequently have 30 or more students at a time; a teacher might not notice or could not immediately attend to him. Therefore, Eddie must be taught to persist under less-than-optimal and uncertain reinforcement conditions. If consequences are unpredictable in the generalization setting, they need to be unpredictable in the training setting to ensure a higher probability of maintained responding. Mrs. Claire decided to teach Eddie how to raise his hand, wait to be called on, and try again later if a teacher was unavailable: Eddie would count slowly to 30 while his hand was raised, and if the teacher did not notice, he would lower his hand and try again later. Exploit functional contingencies A contingency is the when-if-then relation that exists between the behavior and the antecedents and consequences. To maximize the probability that a newly acquired behavior may be demonstrated under different circumstances, teachers should be aware of the circumstances in which the target behavior is expected to occur in the generalization setting. If the generalization setting is not likely to reinforce the behavior, consistently reinforces a competing behavior, or punishes a newly acquired behavior, no amount of training is going to transfer the behavior change. Contact natural consequences.  Before any consideration of how a skill should be taught, teachers should first consider what is being taught and whether the skill meets the needs of the student and will be reinforced naturally. Students want to know how a skill is going to benefit them: "What's in it for me?" A best practice is teaching behaviors only if they are likely to contact reinforcement in natural environments — the relevance-of-behavior rule (Ayllon & Azrin, 1968). Mrs. Claire scheduled observations in Eddie's general education classrooms and verified that hand raising was the primary means most students used to obtain teacher assistance. Reinforce generalization.  Sometimes a student must continue to behave as instructed even if the natural environment does not provide sufficient reinforcement. Preference assessments, behavior contracts, daily progress reports and token economies can motivate the student, but must be used with discretion — any artificial reinforcement system should be carefully and systematically faded, when possible, to avoid dependence on the system at the expense of natural reinforcement. Mrs. Claire's preference assessment showed Eddie would like extra computer time, and she offered 5 minutes per question asked in class. Modify maladaptive consequences.  Teachers should consider behaviors already being reinforced in the generalization setting that compete with the trained behavior, and consequences that reduce, eliminate or punish it. From conversations with Eddie, Mrs. Claire learned that some kids get made fun of for asking too many questions in class, so she asked Eddie's teachers to monitor student reactions to his participation and assist as needed. Incorporate functional mediators Despite strong instructional design and delivery with carefully planned behavior management systems in place, generalized responding may still fail to occur. Mediation strategies may be needed to bridge the gap between training and generalization settings. Two procedures receive special attention in the literature (Stokes & Osnes, 1989). Incorporate common environmental stimuli.  It is recommended that the training setting be as similar in form and function to the intended generalization setting as possible. This may require altering the physical arrangement of the training setting to mirror the generalization setting. Incorporating common personnel among the settings may help as well: if a general education teacher or students from the general education class are able to participate in training, all the better. The more features the two settings have in common, the greater the probability that generalization will occur. Mrs. Claire scheduled time in the library to train with the laptops Eddie would use in social studies, and recruited Mr. Harris to model the traffic light signal system. Incorporate self-mediated physical, verbal, and covert stimuli.  Self-management interventions may serve as remote prompts to remind a student what to do: listing the steps required to solve a problem, a reminder card taped to a student's desk in both settings, electronic timers such as a MotivAider or a smartphone application, self-management checklists and mnemonic memory aids. The common theme is the transfer of the role of the teacher to the student. Mrs. Claire modified Eddie's daily progress report to list the steps for obtaining assistance, with a starred reminder about Mr. Harris's class, and taught Eddie to self-monitor — recording each attempt with an open circle, shading it in when successful, and presenting the results to the teacher at the end of class for verification and feedback. How it went Mrs. Claire sent Eddie off to his first class: science with Mr. Harris. After 50 long minutes, Eddie returned to check in. With his head down and his self-monitoring form squashed in his hand, Eddie approached. "How'd it go?" she asked nervously. Eddie smiled and handed her the form. "Can I use the swivel chair for my computer time?" he asked. Mrs. Claire saw three open circles and one closed circle next to Mr. Harris's initials, followed by about 30 exclamation points. It was only then that Mrs. Claire realized the reward of 5 minutes of computer time for every hand raise was way too much time. Recommendations and conclusion Programming for generalization is perhaps one of the most challenging tasks for behavior interventionists (Hayes, Rincover, & Solnick, 1980), because much of the behavioral process involved with generalization is unknown. The following recommendations serve as a summary to guide practitioners' efforts (Cooper et al., 2007, pp. 650–651): Minimize the need for generalization as much as possible.  Access to a student's least restrictive environment is not just a federal requirement; it is best practice for generalization promotion. Conducting instruction in the environments within which a student is expected to perform the skill eliminates the need for generalization promotion strategies in the first place. Conduct generalization probes before, during, and after instruction.  Close, continual contact with relevant outcome data (Bushell & Baer, 1994) is a hallmark of applied behavior analysis. Generalization, as with any academic or social skill objective, requires consistent formative data collection. Involve significant others whenever possible.  Incorporating parents, teachers, staff, or other students from the generalization settings in initial instruction serves much the same purpose as programming common stimuli. The most relevant controlling stimuli from a generalization setting are often the people with whom our students interact; bringing those individuals into the instructional setting also teaches others to be more receptive to the target behavior. Promote generalization with the least intrusive and least costly methods possible.  Avoid unnecessary use of artificial reinforcement. If a behavior is to be functional in natural settings, it must be brought under the control of natural schedules of reinforcement; whatever additional reinforcers are used to initially teach a skill must eventually be faded. Contrive intervention approaches as needed to achieve important generalized outcomes.  If generalization promotion is the ultimate goal, teachers should employ whatever strategies are necessary within the categories of train diversely, exploit functional contingencies, and mediate generalization. The ability of teachers' efforts to produce generalization outcomes is crucial to the development of independent learners capable of succeeding in the real world.
